idiom_name: recursive task split over a pool of workers with per-worker deques and work stealing
implementation_notes: Language-neutral structure: represent each problem as a task that either solves a leaf range directly or splits into subtasks; fork the subtasks into the current worker's deque, then join them and combine their results. Workers own a deque each and pop their own newest task (depth-first, good locality) while idle workers take the oldest task of a random victim (breadth-first, usually the biggest remaining unit of work). The scheduler must let a worker that reaches a join keep executing other tasks or stealing until the awaited task completes, instead of blocking on a condition variable - that single rule is what separates a fork/join pool from a pool that deadlocks under recursion. Stop splitting at a granularity threshold tuned to the workload; keep subtasks independent (results return through joins, never through shared mutable state). Choosing a stock runtime (ForkJoinPool, TPL, rayon, TBB, Go runtime, OpenMP tasks) beats hand-rolling the deques unless the platform has none.
code_sketch:
solve(problem):
    if small(problem):                    # granularity threshold
        return direct(problem)
    parts = split(problem)                # decompose
    for p in parts: push_task(p)          # fork into the local deque
    return combine(join(parts))           # join: wait for subtasks, combine results
# worker loop:
#   pop newest local task; if none, steal oldest from another worker; else idle/block
pitfalls: A join that blocks the worker instead of helping with other tasks stalls the pool under deep recursion - joins must be cooperative.
Sibling tasks sharing mutable accumulators turn the combine step into a data race; results must flow back through joins.
A pool built per call instead of per process multiplies workers, destroys locality and oversubscribes the machine.

Wrong move: running blocking JDBC/HTTP calls inside parallelStream() or CompletableFuture defaults -> every ForkJoinPool.commonPool worker parks on I/O and unrelated fork/join work in the same JVM starves (OpenJDK tracks common-pool starvation as a real failure mode, JDK-8315740) -> instead dispatch blocking calls to a dedicated executor, or confine the CPU-bound stream to a private pool via pool.submit(streamOp).get().

Wrong move: reading getStealCount()/getQueuedTaskCount() as scheduling guarantees -> the values are undercounts unless the pool is quiescent and steering is deliberately unfair between competing workloads -> instead rely only on fork/join semantics for correctness and use the counters for coarse tuning, giving latency-critical jobs their own pool.

Wrong move: treating rayon::join or ForkJoinTask.fork as a place to await external events -> join blocks a worker thread that then cannot steal, so I/O waits or inter-task dependencies starve the pool -> instead keep leaf tasks CPU-bound and push waiting to the runtime's async mechanism (async/await, futures on a separate dispatcher).
